Areas/Tech-Stack/Java.title: Java
Areas/Tech-Stack/Java.content:
What is Java?
Basics
Java is a - strongly typed - compiled programming language.
Its compiled into bytecode which is interpreted by the JVM which makes java programs very portable when comparing it with for example: C/C++.
Every reference type in Java is a class that inherits from the Object.
Everything in Java is passed by value even object references, meaning:
This means that when passing an object to a value you are passing a copy of the object reference.
So even if you change that reference within the method, the original object is not changed.
Dog d = new Dog("Max"); Foo(d); System.out.println(d.getName()); // will still print Max (in C++(where you can pass by reference) it would print Brian) (...) . public void Foo(Dog dog) {   dog = new Dog("Brian"); }
Abstractions
We can implement Abstractions using both Interfaces and Abstract classes.
Interfaces
Interfaces are certain structures that allow you to declare certain responsibilities that classes implementing the interface have to define.
NOTE
Good class design says that objects should define what responsibilities they want supplied, not how they want them to be satisfied. That is where interfaces come in.
Example
Say we are using a ledger class that stores records. Each ledger needs something to provide searching through them.
So we provide a Finder class via constructor.
public Ledger(Finder finder){ ... }
Now if we for instance find a better implementation of the finder ex. Finder2 we have to manually replace each Finder occurrence.
A better way to do it is to use an interface IFinder and use it like so:
public Ledger(IFinder finder){ ... }
Java Database connectivity
A set of abstractions provided by the JDK to allow connections to databases.

Projects/Writing/learning.title: On types of learning.
Projects/Writing/learning.content:
Background
Wondering around the library today, one book took my attention. 
It was the “Introduction to Programming in Java: An Interdisciplinary Approach” by Robert Sedgewick. 
Huge around 800 pages long book. Looking at it, made me imagine going through it.
I wondered about how many great insights are in there to get from such an experienced teacher and scientist?
Even though I’m much beyond the introductory courses to programming,  how much insight could i gather?
But then I though about how long it would take. How artificial would solving these little example problems feel.
How again, I would be learning not from the feedback from the real world but from the comments of a teacher
And then i thought about the alternative. About building projects that interest me. About creating and validating my knowledge as I go as opposed to amassing facts that I don’t use, of importance that I don’t get.
Thesis
Two types of learning rely on these principles:

Learning theory is a prerequisite to practice


Memorizing and following a teacher. Trusting him on authority. Preparing yourself thoroughly before facing actual tasks.


Learning theory is to supplement and improve practice


Focus on building and learn theory on a need-to basis, validating different approaches by the collision with the real world with disregard to authority.

In a Dockerfile, instruction order matters. 
Write instructions that are not bound to change earlier, and those that change more frequently later. 
Because if docker detects a change, it won’t use cached values for the present or any further instructions.

Resources/Infrastructure/Kubernetes_cont.title: Kubernetes controllers
Resources/Infrastructure/Kubernetes_cont.content:
Simply
Controller is a Kubernetes object which communicates with it’s API. 
Validating present state of the cluster and making changes to keep in line with specifications.

How do controllers keep track of the state of the cluster?


using labels which are created at build-time/runtime and can also be altered.
Altering labels can lead to deployments:

Abandoning a pod (by changing the expected label to something else). This should force the deployment to create a new pod.
Adopting a pod (by changing label of somepod to the one expected by a deployment). 
This should force the deployment to delete a pod  if a node is healthy(has the expected amount of pods).



Types

Deployments make sure that the specified amount of pods with specific labels are running, they recreate a pod if it goes offline, terminate a pod if it’s excess.

Resources/Infrastructure/Linux.title: Linux
Resources/Infrastructure/Linux.content:
Definition
Linux is an operating system kernel.
Meaning it defines the core structure, layout of the operating system and the way it manages computer-user interaction.
User input is handled first by the shell.
Distributions
Linux Distributions are operating systems that are built on top of the Linux kernel.
There are different kinds of distributions:

Stable (updating the OS requires reinstalling it)
Rolling-release (updates happen periodically)
Atomic (The updates are rolled out atomically, usually as images)
Immutable (the base OS can’t be modified)

Examples:

OpenSUSE Tumbleweed - a rolling release distro.
Fedora - something between stable and rolling-release.

Resources/Programming/Spring_bean_scopes.title: Spring_bean_scopes
Resources/Programming/Spring_bean_scopes.content:
What are the scopes of a spring object?
In default Spring objects managed by the context(beans), have two scopes of existence, singleton (the default) and prototype. With Spring Web we increase that to five scopes (singleton,  prototype, session, app, request).
Singleton scope
Do not mistake for the singleton pattern!
Singleton scope means that only one instance of a bean is created per Spring container. However Spring allows having many singleton beans of the same class, if each has a different beanID.
Prototype scope
Each time a bean is called, a new instance is created.
Additional Spring Web scopes
session
New instance of a bean is created for each session and persist through that session.
app
A bean instance is created when the app is ran initially, persists across sessions.
request
A new instance of a bean is created for each http request. Exists only for that specific http request.

Resources/Security/Cyber_security.title: Cyber Security
Resources/Security/Cyber_security.content:
Associated terms

White hat hacking / ethical hacking - hacking done purposely for the sake of analyzing vulnerabilities in a system.
Unauthorized / authorized layer - the separation of a system, to the part available to authorized users and the part available to unauthorized users.
Authentication - The verification of use’s identity. We can differentiate between many different types of Authentication for example: Credential based(password and email), Two Factor auth: (card and pin), Hardware based:(car key).
Authorization - Allowing/Disallowing the usage of a certain resource based on the user’s identity.

Basic security checklist

 One security breach is enough to compromise the whole system?
 The sensitive data is encrypted and masked?
 Is SSL security enabled?

Resources/Security/HashCorp_vault.title: HashCorp_vault
Resources/Security/HashCorp_vault.content:
Why?
The core idea is the centralization of secret management.

Prevent “sprawl” - holding secrets in many different, mostly insecure places.


Allow the usage of certain secrets only to certain groups.
Track the use of secrets.
Ensure encryption on site and in transit.


Save secrets from apps, because we consider all of them insecure by design (logging systems etc.).


ephemeral secrets ex. keys regenerated every 10 days.
unique for each user (allow for pinpointing the attack direction)


Reduce security concerns from poorly implemented cryptography by developers.

CLI
Startup

vault server (OPTIONS) - create the vault
export VAULT_ADDR=(copied address)
export VAULT_CACERT=(copied certified authority file path) you will only be able to use the vault if you have 2.,3.
vault login - you will be prompted to enter the token you’ve chosen at the vault creation.
vault status
 pkill vault - kill vault from anywhere
 UNSET VAULT_CACERT VAULT_ADDR

Areas/Climbing/Climbing.title: Climbing
Areas/Climbing/Climbing.content:
Alright first things first, as of right now I’ve been climbing at most three times.
But truth be it got a hold on me, why? Well I think maybe because of how it represent freedom.
Since I remember I wanted to live unconstrained, not in the abolish-morality-Nietzche-way, but in the not-constrained-by-money-and-societal-norms way. Moving along the z-axis is one of the most badass ways to feel your physical freedom while at the same time interacting with nature, overcoming your fears and shortcomings.
Even though I really haven’t been in any high mountains, the mere sight or talk of them puts me in awe. I feel they allow for quality contemplations in solitude, escaping the rush and external pressure.
Or the other possibility is simply that If I weren’t a human I would want to be a monkey and I read Kokou no Hito quite recently.
